# Abstract {.unnumbered}

This exploratory study examines employer-industry classification as a data-quality component of a career evaluation product for healthcare data analysts. It reconstructs a 2017 study and adapts its approach to a local Jobs_2026 snapshot. A scan of 2,350,355 records yielded 362 eligible employers for classification and 112 postings for a January–September 2026 US career benchmark. Employer-name-disjoint evaluation produced positive-class F1 scores of 0.553 for a linear SVM and 0.717 for GBDT. These scores measure agreement with dataset-derived labels rather than independently established employer truth. SQL appeared in 63 career postings; sparse salary evidence and missing work-arrangement fields restricted recommendations. The contribution is a reproducible, scoped analysis with explicit label and coverage limitations. It does not establish national hiring patterns or personal skill deficits.

**Keywords:** employer industry classification; job postings; healthcare data analysts; NAICS; career evaluation; data quality.

# Introduction

This report reconstructs @goindani2017 and applies their employer-industry classification approach to Jobs_2026 [@jobs2026]. The career audience is students targeting healthcare data analyst roles in NAICS sector 62. The new analysis provides a selected-sample market benchmark and classifier evaluation, with explicit limitations on label quality and personal skill assessment.

The analysis ran locally at the user's request. This departs from the supplied course guides' assigned EC2 requirement. No public deployment or independently reviewed employer truth is claimed.

{{< include _content/research-framing.md >}}

# Original study and reconstruction

The paper aggregates normalized job titles and employer-name keywords to predict Transportation or Health Care industry membership. It uses within-employer title shares, a 1% title cutoff, positive-class significance and frequency thresholds, and SVM or GBDT models. Reported collection covers April–June 2017 and an initial sample of 10,000 employers.

The legacy system has higher classification F-scores on defined employers, while GBDT provides greater utility for finding undefined employers than SVM. Classification and error discovery evaluate different outcomes.

# Materials and methods

The source is a local snapshot of 97 Jobs_2026 partitions [@jobs2026]. Records must fall in January–September 2026, have an explicit US country value and recognized industry sector, and not be explicitly flagged as staffing. Posting IDs define duplicates. Employer-name groups require at least 20 eligible postings and an 80% dominant-sector share. The career benchmark additionally requires sector 62 and the declared analyst-title pattern.

Following the feature concept in @goindani2017, title shares and employer-name words represent each employer. Vocabulary thresholds are fitted only on training employers. The adaptation uses scikit-learn [@pedregosa2011], stratified train/validation/test partitions and validation F1 to select settings. The endpoint is agreement with supplied sector labels. Independent adjudication and the original undefined-employer utility endpoint are unavailable. The results below provide the filtering ledger, split counts and model details.

# Discussion and career implications

SQL appears in 63 of 112 selected postings. Tableau appears in 36; Power BI, Python and Excel each appear in 26. These frequencies support prioritizing SQL and a visualization tool for a sample-relevant learning portfolio. They do not establish individual deficiencies or the causal effect of training on job placement.

The sample contains 24 explicitly remote and 20 hybrid postings, with 58 unknown. Check each listing before recommending it as a remote option. The largest known state counts are Virginia, New York and California, but missing geography and selection prevent population-level rankings. Three usable currency-explicit salary observations are too few for a headline salary recommendation.

A proposed opportunity scorecard weights demand 25%, salary 20%, accessibility 20%, skill fit 25% and remote flexibility 10%. These weights are illustrative. A composite ranking is withheld because personal profiles and adequate salary coverage are missing. The completed analytical track is employer-industry classification, with metrics and confusion matrices above.

# Limitations and next validation

This is an exploratory adaptation, not an exact replication of the proprietary 2017 system. Input coverage, missing country and industry fields, noisy labels, title matching, unresolved aliases and missing salary evidence affect the sample. Dataset-derived labels cannot independently validate the employer knowledge base. Personal profiles, human team contributions, standup records and public hosting are outside the completed evidence.

Review original requirements and a sample of model agreement and disagreement cases. Resolve aliases and test a later time period before filtering opportunities by predictions. Reproduce on EC2 if submitting under the original course rules.

# Conclusion

Posting-derived features recover part of the dataset's employer-industry signal, but missed healthcare employers and unverified target labels limit automatic filtering. The career subset supports a sample-specific emphasis on SQL and visualization skills. Stronger recommendations require better compensation coverage, independent review and, for personal advice, assessed participant profiles.
